turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Botha, in you come. Have a seat. What's the problem today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, doctor, the parking was hectic, we sat at that robot by the mall for ages, and Thandi wouldn't let me get out. But ja, it's the burning again when I pass urine.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Burning when you pass urine. How many times this year?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): This is the third time this year. Um, well, actually, maybe the fourth, if I count February. That one went away quick.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): This bout. How many days?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. It started Wednesday. Or, hang on, Wednesday was Pick n Pay. Ja, three days, I'm pretty sure.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, she told me on Sunday already. That's five days, not three.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday was the braai, Thandi. My eyes were stinging from the smoke, that's all. The urine burning is three days. I think.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So roughly three to six days. I won't nail it further. Any blood in the urine?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No blood that I've seen.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Passing urine more often than usual?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): All the time, hey. I was squirming in the car.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): At night?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Two times. No, two or three times a night. I was up again.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I counted four times last night. The passage light woke me each time.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok, four then. I lose track when I'm half asleep.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Thandi put the thermometer on me yesterday and it was normal.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain in the back, or in the side over the kidney?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Back's fine. I can still bend to the oven.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vaginal discharge, itching, or a bad smell?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Definitely not.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Taken anything for it?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, shame, I shouldn't have, my sister Liesl left amoxicillin, those two-fifty ones, from her tooth. No, wait, I'm mixing it up, it was ciprofloxacin, five hundred milligrams I think, twice a day for this burning.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): For how many days?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. Ag, no, two days. I finished them on Tuesday, swallowed the last one with my tea.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She skipped the evening tablet, doctor. Both nights. I put it in the dish and it was still there in the morning.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I forgot once. Well, actually, maybe both nights. Don't look at me like that, my head's full.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): What do you take regularly?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): A little white pill for my blood pressure, I can never remember the silly name. And simvastatin for the cholesterol, ten milligrams... no, twenty milligrams, at night.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That white tablet, the label's rubbed off. I thought it was perindopril, then I thought amlodipine. I really couldn't say.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. The blood pressure and the cholesterol. How long on the pressure one?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Since my sixties. I'm seventy-one now, so years and years. Thandi lives in with me, she tries to keep the pills straight.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the simvastatin, how long?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Five years? Ja, about five years. My late husband was on the same one, funny enough.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Speaking of him, he lived for the cricket. Did you see the Proteas on Saturday? I nearly fell off the couch.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I didn't watch it.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, man, just quickly. That catch at midwicket. Thandi was shouting at the television.
[SEG0039] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I was shouting because of the volume, not the cricket. I don't follow it.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): You do so. You asked me who was bowling. And my grandson Liam, he's nine, he bowls in the yard with a tennis ball and knocks the pot plants over.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Botha, we should...
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): And then Eskom cut us in the middle of the over. Load shedding, stage four, right when they needed a boundary. Candles out like it's nineteen eighty.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The candles are in the sideboard. We were fine.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, and the neighbour's Jack Russell went mad in the dark. Yaps at the gate every time a bakkie goes past.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I need to finish.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, sorry. The drive home will be just as bad, school traffic and all. Liam's concert is on Thursday, he's a tree, a paper tree.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We'll talk about the concert later, Maggie.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The weather's been lovely for it, though. Not too hot, a breeze off the mountain. I told him he'll wilt if he stands in the sun in that costume.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back to you, please.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. I ramble when I'm nervous. It's embarrassing, this whole visit.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, about what you asked, down below, I didn't want to say it. There is a bit of itching on the outside, not discharge. And I don't have a smell, that part was true.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Itching on the outside only. The burning is still when the urine comes?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The burning is when the urine comes, and the itch is on the skin, separate. It's mild, more annoying than sore.
[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Are you sexually active?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm a widow. Not for years. Nothing like that.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to stamp one label on this yet. It may be another bladder infection, possibly the fourth this year, or it may be irritation on the vaginal side, the itch. I am not calling it a sexually transmitted infection, and I won't decide until we see what the urine shows.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it dangerous? My neighbour had a kidney business and she was in hospital a week, on a drip, the whole story. I don't want that.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't say that from this chat. I'm sending a midstream urine for microscopy and culture. The lab sister at the hatch will give you the pot.
[SEG0059] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Must I go in with her for the sample?
[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): If she wants you there, yes. And nobody takes another antibiotic out of a relative's cupboard.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't. Liesl's pills are finished anyway. I felt silly even starting them.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drink plenty of water today and tomorrow.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Water, ja. Not my rooibos? I live on rooibos, six cups, easy.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Water is what I want. Rooibos won't harm you, but it doesn't count as the water.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Ok. And if this carries on?
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back if you're still burning in three days. Sooner if you get a fever or pain in the back, though you haven't got those now.
[SEG0067] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll bring her back if it isn't settling. I've got the car most mornings.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Mornings Thandi does Checkers. We always get the rotisserie chicken, and if Liam is with us he eats half before we're home.
[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's between you and Liam. Do the urine before you leave. The form goes to reception.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Reception, ja. The lady with the red glasses was sharp about my medical aid last month. I nearly wrote a letter to the manager.
[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not my department. Questions about what I've said?
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): The cipro. Did I mess the test up by taking it already?
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can muddy the culture. We still send the urine. I'm not starting another antibiotic today.
[SEG0074] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Thank you, doctor. We'll do the bottle on the way out.
[SEG0075] person_2 (PATIENT): If the Proteas win tonight and I miss it, I'm blaming this queue. Only joking. Thanks, hey.
[SEG0076] person_1 (DOCTOR): On you go. Reception has the form.

spec.situation: Woman with burning urine again; says 'third time this year' then corrects to 'maybe the fourth'; took leftover antibiotic from a sister; embarrassed; vaginal symptoms denied, then partly admitted. Urine test ordered.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.

bad.text: ciprofloxacin (dose=500 mg, frequency=twice daily, duration=2 days, indication=burning when passing urine, status=discontinued, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Urinary frequency had a key detail: the patient said she was passing urine 'all the time' and was squirming in the car.
The patient reported that the outside itching was separate from the dysuria, on the skin only, with burning specifically when urine comes.

The patient denied vaginal itching initially, but later corrected this and said there is a bit of itching on the outside only, mild, with no discharge and no smell. The initial denial of itching is recorded only as a final positive symptom and could miss the corrected history context.
The patient said she had no blood in the urine that she had seen, not an absolute denial of haematuria.
There was a normal thermometer reading yesterday when fever was asked about.

Ciprofloxacin adherence detail is incomplete: caregiver said both evening tablets were missed, patient said she forgot once and maybe both nights, so the actual taken frequency may have been less than twice daily.
The patient first confused the borrowed antibiotic with amoxicillin before correcting to ciprofloxacin; this uncertainty about exactly what she took is not recorded.
The patient asked whether prior ciprofloxacin might have affected the urine test, and the doctor said it can muddy the culture but they would still send the urine.
The doctor explicitly stated he was not starting another antibiotic today.
The doctor explicitly said he was not calling this a sexually transmitted infection.
Hydration advice was more specific: drink plenty of water today and tomorrow; rooibos would not harm her but did not count as the water he wanted.
